newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Japan seeks to broaden ties with Southeast Asia.
newsitem.headline: Japan seeks to broaden ties with Southeast Asia.

text.p: Japan's proposals to enhance non-economic ties with a newly assertive Southeast Asia aim to broaden a relationship based on Tokyo's position as number one business partner in the region, analysts said on Tuesday.

Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, in a speech on Tuesday in Singapore, called for regular summits between Japan and regional leaders, joint efforts on preserving traditional Southeast Asian cultures and collaboration on global concerns such as terrorism and the environment.

Hashimoto's speech capped a week-long visit to Malaysia, Indonesia, Brunei, Vietnam and Singapore -- five of the seven countries in the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN), which also includes Thailand and the Philippines.
The visit came at a time when ASEAN has emerged as an important bloc in the post-Cold War lineup and when Japan is trying to shoulder new global responsibilities, analysts said.

"Japan is keen to play a larger international role. Hashimoto also sees the increasing role of ASEAN and so in that sense Japan sees the need to work together with ASEAN," said Stephen Leong, executive director of the Centre for Japan Studies in Kuala Lumpur.
The visit also came as Japan faced criticism over its bloated trade surpluses with Southeast Asia and the slow pace of its technology transfers.
About 16 percent of Japan's total trade is with ASEAN members and Japan is the region's biggest foreign investor.
Japan's ambassador to Malaysia, Taizo Nakamura, in a 1995 speech expressed concern that Japan's importance in Southeast Asia appeared to be declining.

Nakamura said this was due to frequent changes in Japan's government, a lingering recession, its ambivalence to an exclusive East Asia trade forum and reduced need for Japanese aid after the region's rapid development.
In the 1970s, anti-Japanese riots swept Indonesia and Thailand after Japan first acquired a visible economic presence in the region.

Although anti-Japanese sentiment has all but disappeared since then, a certain wariness still persists in the region about a nation that conquered Southeast Asia in World War Two in the name of Japan's Greater Co-Prosperity Sphere.

"We think Japan should take a more active role in regional and international affairs as long as it is under multi-lateral organisations," said Dewi Fortuna Anwar, regional affairs analyst at the Indonesian Institute of Sciences.
Hashimoto said he won agreement from the leaders he had met during his tour for regular Japan-ASEAN summits, which he told a news conference should be held at least once a year.
Some analysts questioned the wisdom of such summits.
"I don't know if it will be really necessary at the moment, as you are creating a precedent and the United States and China will want (summits)," Anwar said. "There will be too many summits."
Hashimoto also called for closer cooperation at the United Nations, where Japan is about to take a seat on the Security Council for two years.
China, which many analysts believe will overtake Japan as the biggest economy in Asia next century, loomed large in Hashimoto's consultations.
In his Singapore speech, Hashimoto called for wide-ranging exchanges with China "so she can secure her position as a constructive partner in the international community".
China has island territorial disputes with several ASEAN countries as well as with Japan.
